extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political economy, economic_history, and public_policy (general educated audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of principles for evaluating coinage policy (seignorage, melting/exportation, mint operations) and the motives and effects of establishing colonies. Provides diagnostic criteria and examples for when particular monetary or colonial policies are advantageous or ruinous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portugal trade facilitates round‑about foreign trade
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal advantage of the Portugal trade lies in facilitating round-about foreign trades of consumption by means of gold and silver, which are universal instruments of commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gold and silver are more readily received in return for commodities, have small bulk and great value (lower transport costs and less loss of value), and so are especially convenient when goods are bought in one foreign country only to be sold or exchanged in another. This is an important, though not capital, advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual importation of bullion primarily serves foreign commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: The great annual importation of gold and silver is neither for plate nor coin but for foreign trade — to facilitate consumption trades abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because bullion is convenient for round-about trade, import flows of gold/silver should be interpreted as trade-facilitating rather than direct additions to domestic plate or coin stocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Net additions to plate are small; much new plate from melted old plate
rubrics_metrics.description: The greater part of new plate sold by goldsmiths is made from other old plate melted down; thus the annual addition to the kingdom's plate is small and requires only a very small annual importation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy or worries premised on large annual additions to plate (necessitating large bullion imports) are misplaced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coinage largely replaces worn coin rather than adding new money
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of the annual coinage replaces the best part of the circulating coin which is daily melted down; the mint often repairs wear rather than creating real additions to currency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coin is received by weight, new coin rarely increases practical circulating money because new pieces are mixed with worn coin; the mint's daytime work is undone at night by melting for bullion profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profit from melting newly coined money when bullion market > mint price
rubrics_metrics.description: If market bullion prices exceed the mint price equivalent of newly coined money, there is an evident profit in melting down new coin and selling as bullion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: new guineas containing full standard weight could be melted and sold for between £47:14s and £48 when mint price equated to £46:14:6; this incentivises instantaneous melting despite government precautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seignorage raises coin value relative to bullion and can deter melting/export
rubrics_metrics.description: A seignorage (coinage duty) increases the market value of coin above the pure bullion value; if it's moderate, it is an effective preventive of melting and exportation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seignorage equal to or above the difference between standard and actual currency weight eliminates profit from melting; examples illustrate outcomes for seignorage rates (5%, 2%, 1%) relative to a 2% deficit in coin weight. Excessive seignorage, however, risks encouraging counterfeiting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exorbitant seignorage risks counterfeiting; deterrence depends on enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: If seignorage is excessive (far above real coinage cost), the large spread between bullion and coin value may encourage counterfeiters to enter the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether high seignorage creates counterfeiting depends on the dangers faced by false coiners; in France an 8% seignorage exists without notable counterfeiting because penalties/difficulties deter criminals.

rubrics_metrics.name: When coin is received by tale, seignorage most effectively prevents melting/export
rubrics_metrics.description: Where money is received by tale (nominal count) rather than by weight, seignorage is the most effectual preventive of melting and exportation, because it offsets the profit from inferior-weight circulating coin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The heaviest/best coins are the ones commonly melted or exported, so seignorage reduces incentives on those pieces and stabilises circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government-paid coinage is forgone revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: When government defrays the expense of coinage it not only incurs small expense but also loses revenue it could have collected via a proper duty (seignorage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even modest annual savings (e.g., £18–20k) in events that can recur justify attention; governments granting free coinage are effectively giving up revenue and possible policy tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of coin degradation on bank and mint economics
rubrics_metrics.description: If circulating coin is below standard weight, those who bring bullion to mint (notably the Bank of England) may lose on bullion purchases unless seignorage compensates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: with currency 2% below standard and no seignorage, banks paid 2% more for bullion to coin than coin was worth in circulation; with a seignorage equal to the deficiency the bank's net position would be unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate seignorage does not ultimately increase expense for bullion‑depositors
rubrics_metrics.description: When seignorage is moderate (not encouraging false coining), those who advance the tax (merchants) get it back in price — for money, however, there is no final consumer so the tax is advanced but not finally borne by anyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus moderate seignorage does not increase bank or private persons' expense for coinage and can serve public revenue and policy purposes without burdening them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom of weighing coin matters for distribution of gains/losses
rubrics_metrics.description: If the custom of weighing gold coin continues, the bank gains little from seignorage; but if receiving by tale becomes common and coin degrades, imposing seignorage could produce considerable savings for the bank.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional practices (weighing vs tale) affect incentives and distribution of costs between government, banks, and merchants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonies: motives differ by historical context (Greek, Roman, modern Europe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek colonies were driven by overpopulation and the search for new habitations and became independent states; Roman colonies were plantations within conquered territories serving as garrisons and remained subject to the mother city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding colonial motives requires attention to the demographic and political conditions that prompted settlement: necessity/utility for ancients versus different incentives for modern European colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: European American colonies were motivated chiefly by hopes of treasure (gold)
rubrics_metrics.description: The establishment of European colonies in America and the West Indies arose not from necessity and their utility was not clearly understood at first; the primary motive was the expectation of finding gold and precious metals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Columbus and subsequent adventurers emphasised mineral riches to secure royal support; the pious purpose of conversion was used to sanctify the project, but economic hunger for precious metals was the driving force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overstating discoveries' value helps secure sponsoring support
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing newly discovered lands as exceptionally valuable (e.g., St. Domingo as abounding in gold) was useful and often necessary to obtain royal backing and resources for colonization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Columbus proposed that half of all wealth found belong to the crown; such promises incentivised sponsorship but could be unsustainable once easy plunder was exhausted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaction and taxation can lead to rapid resource depletion and abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Rigorous exaction (taxation) of mines caused the abandoning of mines (e.g., St. Domingo) once easy plunder was exhausted, because heavy dues removed incentive to work mines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxation regimes that take too large a share of gross produce can render resource exploitation uneconomic; historical reductions of crown shares (from half to twentieth) illustrate adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for new mines is a high-risk, often ruinous speculative project
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects searching for new gold and silver mines are probably the most disadvantageous lottery: few prizes but expensive tickets, commonly absorbing both capital and expected return.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prudent lawgiver seeking to increase national capital should avoid extraordinary encouragement of mining projects since they often destroy capital rather than replace it with ordinary profits of stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colonial ventures often driven by individual avidity, not sober judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite poor long-run expectations for mining projects, human avidity leads many to overinvest in uncertain enterprises; where success probability exists, too much private capital tends to flow towards these ventures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers should account for psychological incentives that lead to over-allocation of capital to speculative colonial projects.
